If the means of reducing the weight of vehicles by 50 pounds is costly, it can be assumed that it would only be applied to 10 percent of the vehicles and the cost possibly spread over all vehicles. If the cost of the weight reduction is relatively small it can be presumed that the 50 pound weight reduction would be applied to all vehicles because of the resulting marketing benefits and the fact the future weight reductions could cause more inertia weight class shifts. The scenario developed for this standard included relatively low cost methods of reducing weight. If GM improves fuel economy by this means, it is presumed that all vehicles would lose the 50 pounds. Thus, the determination of national resources savings were based on the full application of 50-pound weight reduction to the GM fleet.
Another area of impact on natural resources is an increase in the size of catalytic converters and the resultant demand for platinum and palladium. This impact is applicable only under the assumption that all impacts are attributable to the AFES.
